rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
Under federal law, the protection period before birth covers the last six weeks before delivery. MuSchG §3(1) says the employer may not employ a pregnant woman "in den letzten sechs Wochen vor der Entbindung" (Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung). Six weeks before 15 November 2026 is 4 October 2026. The excerpts do not set out how the first and last days are counted, so confirm the exact first day with your employer.

How the period is set:
- It is calculated from the expected day of delivery shown in the certificate from a doctor, midwife or Entbindungspfleger ("der voraussichtliche Tag der Entbindung … wie er sich aus dem ärztlichen Zeugnis … ergibt").
- If you do not give birth on the expected day, the period before birth becomes shorter or longer to match.
- During this period you may still work if you expressly declare that you are willing to. You can withdraw that declaration at any time, with effect for the future.
- The same six weeks before the due date apply with twins or other multiples (familienportal.de).

After the birth, Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) lasts until eight weeks after delivery (MuSchG §3(2)). It extends to twelve weeks in three cases:
1. premature births,
2. multiple births, and
3. where a disability of the child is medically certified within eight weeks of the birth. This third case applies only if you apply for it.

If the baby is born early, the period after birth is also extended by the time lost before birth. The twelve-week extension does not apply to a stillbirth.

Related points from the excerpts:
- MuSchG §15 says a pregnant woman should tell her employer about the pregnancy and the expected day of delivery as soon as she knows. If the employer asks, she should show a certificate that states the expected day.
- The familienportal page says self-employed women are not covered by the Mutterschutzgesetz.
- SGB V §24i(3) says Mutterschaftsgeld is paid for the protection periods and the day of delivery. For payment before the birth, the certificate from a doctor or midwife stating the expected day of delivery is decisive.
- MuSchG §20 says an employee also receives an employer top-up to Mutterschaftsgeld for the same periods.

Whether these rules apply to you depends on your employment situation. Your employer and your Krankenkasse handle this for your case.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
There is no application deadline in the law. Instead, the law limits back payment. Under BEEG §7(1), Elterngeld (parental allowance) is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the month of life in which the application was received: "rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate vor Beginn des Lebensmonats geleistet, in dem der Antrag auf Elterngeld eingegangen ist."

The months counted are the child's months of life ("Lebensmonate"), starting from the date of birth, not calendar months. Elterngeld can be received from the day of birth (BEEG §4(1)). So the three months of life before the month in which the application arrives are paid. Any earlier months are not. If the application arrives during the child's fourth month of life, the three months before it are the first three months of life. Applications that arrive later lose whole months of payment.

The application must be made in writing ("Elterngeld ist schriftlich zu beantragen", BEEG §7(1)). In the application, you state for which months of life you claim basic Elterngeld, Elterngeld Plus or the partnership bonus.

A similar three-month limit applies if you later change those choices. A change can only be made retroactively for the last three months of life before the month in which the change request was received (BEEG §7(2)).

The source names the Elterngeldstelle as the office that decides on Elterngeld.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)) is requested from your employer, not applied for at an office. How much notice the law requires depends on when the leave falls:

- For leave before your child's third birthday: at the latest seven weeks before it begins ("spätestens sieben Wochen").
- For leave between the third birthday and the end of the child's eighth year: at the latest 13 weeks before it begins ("spätestens 13 Wochen").

The request must be made "in Textform" (BEEG §16(1)). The Familienportal explains that this means a letter without a signature, or an email, is enough.

What the request must contain: if you request leave before the third birthday, you must also state at the same time which periods within two years you will take Elternzeit (BEEG §16(1)).

Exceptions and special cases in the same section:

- Where there are urgent reasons, an appropriately shorter period is exceptionally possible ("Bei dringenden Gründen ist ausnahmsweise eine angemessene kürzere Frist möglich"). The Familienportal gives premature births and adoptive placements that could not be planned in time as examples. It says the period that applies then depends on the individual case.
- If a mother takes Elternzeit directly after the maternity protection period, that protection period counts towards the two-year period. If she takes annual leave between the two, the annual leave counts towards it as well (BEEG §16(1)).
- If a mother cannot request Elternzeit in time to follow directly on from the maternity protection period, for a reason she is not responsible for, she can make the request within one week after that reason ends (BEEG §16(2)).

Related rules:

- Your employer must confirm your Elternzeit to you (BEEG §16(1)).
- You may split your Elternzeit into three periods. More periods need your employer's consent (BEEG §16(1)).
- If you want to work part-time during Elternzeit and claim the legal right to reduced hours, the same notice applies under BEEG §15(7) no. 5. That is seven weeks before the part-time work starts for the period up to the third birthday, and 13 weeks for the period between the third and eighth birthdays, in Textform.
- Protection against dismissal starts from the point at which you requested Elternzeit. It starts no earlier than eight weeks before leave up to the third birthday, and no earlier than 14 weeks before leave between the third and eighth birthdays (BEEG §18(1)).

On earlier births: the Familienportal page says that for children born before 1 July 2015, the seven-week period applies even for leave after the third birthday. The excerpts I was given do not include the statutory provision for those earlier births, so I cannot confirm that rule from the law itself.

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) after the birth is normally eight weeks. Under MuSchG §3(2), the employer may not employ a woman "bis zum Ablauf von acht Wochen nach der Entbindung" (until eight weeks after the birth).

An early birth can extend this in two separate ways.

1. Any birth before the expected date: the six-week period before the birth is shortened, because it runs from the expected date and "verkürzt oder verlängert sich ... entsprechend" when the baby does not arrive on that day (§3(1)). The days lost before the birth are then added to the period after it: "Bei vorzeitiger Entbindung verlängert sich die Schutzfrist nach der Entbindung ... um den Zeitraum der Verkürzung der Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung" (§3(2)). The Familienportal puts it this way: the total stays 14 weeks, and the period after the birth ends as many days after the eight weeks as the baby came before the expected date.

2. A premature birth in the medical sense: the period after the birth is extended to twelve weeks "bei Frühgeburten" (in the case of premature births). The days lost before the birth are added to these twelve weeks as well. The Familienportal says this raises the total from 14 to 18 weeks. It gives a birth weight under 2,500 grams as one example of a birth that counts medically as premature.

The same extension to twelve weeks also applies in two other cases listed in §3(2): multiple births ("bei Mehrlingsgeburten"), and where a disability of the child is medically established before the eight weeks after the birth end. The disability extension applies only if the woman applies for it. The Familienportal says this application is made to the health insurance fund. The twelve-week extension does not apply to a stillbirth.

During the period after the birth, employees may not work even if they want to. A school or university student may resume her training activities early if she expressly asks for it, and may withdraw that request at any time. If an employer demands work during the protection period, the Familienportal says you can turn to your supervisory authority (Aufsichtsbehörde).

Whether a particular birth counts as premature is a medical finding. These sources do not decide it for a given case.

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) for pregnant women is set out in MuSchG §17. There are narrow exceptions, and they need prior approval from a state authority.

When dismissal is not allowed

Under §17(1), dismissal of a woman is not allowed ("Die Kündigung gegenüber einer Frau ist unzulässig") in these periods:

1. during her pregnancy
2. until four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy
3. until the end of her protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth

The employer must know about it

The protection applies if the employer knew of the pregnancy, the miscarriage or the birth when dismissing. It also applies if the employer is told "innerhalb von zwei Wochen nach Zugang der Kündigung" (within two weeks of receiving the dismissal). Missing those two weeks does no harm if:

- the reason was not her fault, and
- she gives the information "unverzüglich" (without delay).

The same rules apply to steps an employer takes to prepare a dismissal.

The Familienportal guidance adds two points:

- The protection applies even if you did not yet know you were pregnant, or were not yet sure.
- You must already have been pregnant when you received the dismissal.

The exception

Under §17(2), "die für den Arbeitsschutz zuständige oberste Landesbehörde oder die von ihr bestimmte Stelle" (the highest state authority for occupational safety, or the body it designates) can, in special cases, exceptionally declare a dismissal permissible. Those cases must have no connection to the woman's condition during pregnancy, after a miscarriage after the twelfth week, or after the birth. The dismissal must be in writing and must state the reason.

The Familienportal page gives these as examples of such special reasons:

- the company is insolvent
- the business is partly shut down
- in a small business, the business cannot continue without a qualified replacement
- the employee has committed a particularly serious breach of duty

In these cases the employer must apply in writing to the supervisory authority. The page says that without that authority's approval, the dismissal is invalid ("Ohne die Zustimmung der Aufsichtsbehörde ist die Kündigung unwirksam").

If you are dismissed anyway

The Familienportal page says that if you are dismissed without the authority's approval, you must bring a claim before the competent labour court to have the dismissal declared invalid. It says the claim must normally be filed "innerhalb von 3 Wochen … ab Erhalt der schriftlichen Kündigung" (within 3 weeks of receiving the written dismissal). If no claim is filed, the dismissal counts as effective.

On how to file, the page says:

- You can file the claim yourself or through a representative such as a lawyer.
- You can also make it orally, recorded by the court office.
- You should also involve the competent supervisory authority.

If the authority approved the dismissal

You can challenge that approval. Depending on the Bundesland, this is done by objection or by lawsuit. This is a separate procedure. It does not replace the labour court claim.

After the birth

The page also says the special Kündigungsschutz can be extended if you take parental leave after the birth.

Who decides

Whether a particular dismissal is permissible is decided by the state authority responsible for occupational safety, which the guidance calls the supervisory authority. Whether a dismissal is valid is decided by the labour court. The excerpts do not name the specific office in Hessen.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Above a set level of zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income), the right to Elterngeld (parental allowance) lapses entirely. It is not reduced; it falls away.

The statute sets the limit at 175,000 euros. BEEG §1(8) says the entitlement lapses ("Ein Anspruch entfällt") if the person earned a zu versteuerndes Einkommen "in Höhe von mehr als 175 000 Euro" in the last completed tax assessment period before the birth ("im letzten abgeschlossenen Veranlagungszeitraum vor der Geburt des Kindes").

If another person also meets the conditions, for example the other parent living in the same household with the child, the two incomes are added together. The entitlement then lapses if "die Summe des zu versteuernden Einkommens beider Personen mehr als 175 000 Euro beträgt". A single parent's own income alone is measured against the same 175,000 euros.

Taxable income is not gross salary. The official Familienportal explains that gross income is usually considerably higher than zu versteuerndes Einkommen. Special expenses, provision expenses, individual allowances and extraordinary burdens are deducted from total income. Its example is a married couple without children on employment income: a taxable income of 175,000 euros corresponds to roughly 207,000 euros gross. The tax office determines the individual figure, and it appears in the tax assessment notice. The page says that notice for the year before the birth should be attached to the Elterngeld application where one exists.

You can apply even if the notice is not yet available. Under BEEG §8(2), if the assessment for the last completed period is not available and the application indicates the limit will probably not be exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation if the limit turns out to be exceeded. Under BEEG §8(3) No. 1, if it cannot yet be said whether the limit is exceeded, the amount is decided provisionally until proof is supplied.

Earlier births were subject to different, higher limits. The Familienportal page lists earlier cohorts, but the transitional provision of the statute is not among the sources here. So I cannot say which limit governs a birth before the current rule took effect.

Whether your household is above or below the limit, and which limit applies to your child's birth, is decided only by the Elterngeld office for your district. That office is where to ask about your own case.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
BEEG §4 sets the number of months of Elterngeld (parental allowance). It is paid per month of the child's life ("Lebensmonate"), not per calendar month.

Basic allowance months. Parents together have "Anspruch auf zwölf Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld", meaning 12 monthly amounts of basic allowance. If one parent's earned income is reduced in two months of the child's life, the parents together get two further months, the "Partnermonate". That makes 14 months in total. One parent can take at most 12 of the basic months.

Trading basic months for Elterngeld Plus. Instead of one month of basic allowance, a parent can take two months of Elterngeld Plus.

Partnership bonus. On top of the 12 basic months, each parent can receive up to four further monthly amounts under the partnership bonus in §4b. The Familienportal guidance says these are extra Elterngeld Plus months for each parent if both of you work part-time at the same time.

Minimum. A parent only has a claim to Elterngeld if they receive it for at least two months.

Time windows:
- Basic allowance can be received until the child completes the 14th month of life.
- Elterngeld Plus can be received until the child completes the 32nd month of life. From the 15th month it must be taken in consecutive months by at least one parent.
- The Familienportal guidance adds that if there is a month after the 14th in which neither parent receives Elterngeld Plus, none can be received afterwards, even if months remain.
- For adopted children, Elterngeld can be received from when the child is taken in, at most until the child's 8th birthday.

Months that are used up automatically. Months in which a parent receives maternity benefits that count under §3(1) no. 1 to 3 count as basic allowance months for that parent. The same applies to private insurance benefits under §192(5) sentence 2 VVG.

Receiving the basic allowance at the same time. Both parents can receive the basic allowance at the same time only in one of the first 12 months of life. The guidance says such a month uses up two basic months. Under §4(6) this limit does not apply in four cases:
- multiple births;
- premature births within §4(5);
- children with a medically established disability under §2(1) sentence 1 SGB IX;
- children who trigger a sibling bonus under §2a.

Premature births, §4(5). Instead of 12, the parents' joint basic allowance is:
1. 13 months if born at least 6 weeks before the expected delivery date;
2. 14 months if at least 8 weeks before;
3. 15 months if at least 12 weeks before;
4. 16 months if at least 16 weeks before.

The expected date is the one in the doctor's or midwife's certificate. In these four cases, the per-parent maximum rises to 13, 14, 15 or 16 basic months respectively, plus up to four partnership bonus months. The basic allowance can then be received until the child completes the 15th, 16th, 17th or 18th month of life respectively. Elterngeld Plus still runs to the 32nd month, taken consecutively from the 16th, 17th, 18th or 19th month respectively.

These are the general rules. How many months your family actually receives is decided by the Elterngeldstelle responsible for your district.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) is extra Elterngeld Plus for parents who both work part time at the same time.

What the law provides (BEEG §4b):
- If both parents work "nicht weniger als 24 und nicht mehr als 32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats" (an average of 24 to 32 hours a week across the child's month of life) and both meet the conditions of §1, each parent gets one additional monthly amount of Elterngeld Plus for that month. The conditions of §1 are not in the excerpts available here.
- Each parent can receive at most four monthly amounts. It can only be drawn for at least two months of life.
- Both parents must draw it "nur gleichzeitig und in aufeinander folgenden Lebensmonaten": at the same time, in consecutive months of life.
- The consecutive-months requirement still counts as met if it later turns out the conditions were not met in every month applied for (§4b(5)).
- BEEG §4(4) confirms that one parent can receive at most 12 monthly amounts of basic parental allowance plus up to four Partnerschaftsbonus amounts. For premature births, §4(5) raises the basic figure to 13, 14, 15 or 16 monthly amounts, depending on whether the child was born at least 6, 8, 12 or 16 weeks early, still plus up to four Partnerschaftsbonus amounts.

One parent alone (BEEG §4b(4) and §4c):
If, during the bonus, one of the three grounds in §4c(1) arises, one parent can continue alone under §4c(2). The three grounds are:
1. that parent meets the conditions for the single-parent tax relief under §24b(1) and (3) of the Income Tax Act, and the other parent lives with neither that parent nor the child;
2. care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare within the meaning of §1666(1) and (2) of the Civil Code; or
3. care by the other parent is impossible, in particular because of serious illness or severe disability. Economic reasons and being prevented by other activities do not count.
Where one of these grounds applies, a parent who works 24 to 32 hours a week on average in at least two and at most four consecutive months of life gets additional monthly amounts of Elterngeld Plus for those months.

What the federal guidance page adds (Familienportal):
- Separated parents can also receive the Partnerschaftsbonus. Single parents can use it alone, and then only they need to work 24 to 32 hours a week.
- What counts is the average weekly hours over the month, not each individual week. If the average differs from what was planned, this must be reported to the Elterngeldstelle.
- If either parent works under 24 or over 32 hours on average in a month, the bonus for that month must be repaid, and both parents lose it for that month. The other months are not affected if the conditions were met in at least 2 months.
- It can be used before, between or after the other parental allowance months, and also by parents who otherwise only receive basic parental allowance.
- It is calculated in the same way as Elterngeld Plus. Depending on income before the birth, the page gives between 150 and 900 euro per parent per month. rows.question: We forgot to apply for Kindergeld. How far back will they pay?
rows.reply:
Kindergeld (child benefit) is paid retroactively for at most six months. The law says payment is made "rückwirkend nur für die letzten sechs Monate vor Beginn des Monats, in dem der Antrag auf Kindergeld eingegangen ist". That means only the six months before the start of the month in which the Familienkasse receives the application. Months further back are not paid out.

The same provision says the entitlement to Kindergeld itself is not affected by this limit on payment ("bleibt von dieser Auszahlungsbeschränkung unberührt"). The limit is on how far back the money is paid, not on whether the entitlement existed.

The official family portal says retroactive payment applies where Kindergeld was due but not paid, for example because no application was made. When you apply, state in the application that you are applying retroactively and from when you want to receive Kindergeld.

Kindergeld must be applied for in writing. The application should be made to the Familienkasse at your Agentur für Arbeit, which sets and pays Kindergeld. The Familienkasse decides which months are paid in your case. The Bundesagentur für Arbeit's free service line for application questions is 0800 4 555530.

rows.question: How much Kindergeld do we get per month for our first child?

Kindergeld (child benefit) is set by statute at 259 euros per month for each child: "Das Kindergeld beträgt monatlich für jedes Kind 259 Euro" (EStG §66(1); the same wording is in BKGG §6(1)). - Kindergeld is paid monthly from the start of the month in which the conditions are met until the end of the month in which they stop being met (EStG §66(2)). The official guidance gives an example: a child born on 25 May brings the full Kindergeld for May.
- If the tax allowances for children (Freibeträge für Kinder) are raised, Kindergeld is raised accordingly and rounded to whole euros (EStG §66(3), BKGG §6(2)).
- During the year, parents receive Kindergeld. In the annual income tax assessment, the Finanzamt then checks automatically whether the tax allowances for children or the Kindergeld paid is more favourable. No application is needed for this check.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The birth must be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) for the place where the child was born within one week. The statute says the birth is to be reported "binnen einer Woche" to the Standesamt "in dessen Zuständigkeitsbereich es geboren ist" (PStG §18(1)).

The statute names two ways of reporting. The persons named in PStG §19 may report orally or in writing. The institutions named in PStG §20 report in writing. If the child is stillborn, the report must be made "spätestens am dritten auf die Geburt folgenden Werktag", meaning at the latest on the third working day after the birth. Where the persons in §19 report, they must substantiate the birth ("glaubhaft zu machen").

The official Familienportal adds the practical side. If the child was born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the institution notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends the birth certificate from the clinic. If the child was born at home, the midwife or doctor issues that certificate, and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week.

A Familienportal checklist phrases this as "innerhalb von 7 Werktagen" (within 7 working days). The statute says "binnen einer Woche" (within one week), and the statute is what governs.

The Standesamt issues the birth certificate. You need it for applications such as Elterngeld, maternity benefit and health insurance registration. The Standesamt then passes the registration to the residents' registration office automatically.

The Familienportal says to check the website of the Standesamt in the place of birth for any further documents it asks for.

rows.question: What do we need to bring to the Standesamt to register the birth?
rows.reply:
Under PStV §33, when a birth is registered the Standesamt (civil registry office) should ask to see these documents:

1. If the parents are married to each other: their marriage certificate or a certified extract from the marriage register. Their own birth certificates are also needed if the marriage certificate does not show the registration details of the parents' births. The marriage certificate must be shown even if the marriage has ended.
2. If the parents are not married to each other: the mother's birth certificate. If paternity has already been acknowledged, the acknowledgement declarations and the father's birth certificate are also needed, plus any joint custody declarations.
3. An identity card, passport or other recognised passport substitute for the parents.
4. If the birth is reported in person: a certificate of the birth issued by a doctor or midwife who was present at the birth.

The Standesamt can ask for further documents if it needs them to prove the details given.

Who handles the birth certificate from the doctor or midwife depends on where the child was born. If the child was born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the facility notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends the certificate itself. If the child was born at home, the midwife or doctor issues the certificate, and you must present it to the responsible Standesamt within one week.

The responsible Standesamt is the one for the place where the child was born. The Familienportal says you must register the child there "innerhalb 1 Woche" (within one week). Its checklist page says "innerhalb von 7 Werktagen" (within 7 working days).

If both parents are foreign nationals, PStV §34 adds a requirement. When the birth is reported, the Standesamt asks for information on whether a parent has an unlimited right of residence. It may also ask whether a parent holds a residence permit as a Swiss citizen or the family member of one, under the 1999 EU–Switzerland free movement agreement. This information is used to check whether the child acquired German citizenship at birth under StAG §4(3). If the answers indicate these conditions are met, the Standesamt asks the foreigners authority in writing to confirm them. It also asks whether the parent had lived lawfully in Germany for five years at the time of the birth. The Standesamt also asks the foreigners authority if the parents give no information or it doubts the answers.

The Familienportal says the website of the Standesamt in the place where your child is born lists any further documents it needs for registration.

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply:
Yes, statutory health insurance covers midwife care. Under SGB V §24d, an insured woman is entitled to midwife help during pregnancy, at the birth and after the birth ("während der Schwangerschaft, bei und nach der Entbindung Anspruch auf ärztliche Betreuung sowie auf Hebammenhilfe"). This includes the examinations to confirm the pregnancy and prenatal check-ups ("einschließlich der Untersuchungen zur Feststellung der Schwangerschaft und zur Schwangerenvorsorge").

After the birth, the entitlement to Hebamme (midwife) care for the postnatal period lasts until twelve weeks after the birth ("bis zum Ablauf von zwölf Wochen nach der Geburt"). Further care after that needs a doctor's order ("weitergehende Leistungen bedürfen der ärztlichen Anordnung").

If the mother cannot care for the baby after the birth, the insured child has its own entitlement to the midwife services that relate to the child.

The Familienportal confirms that every woman with statutory health insurance has a right to support from a Hebamme. If you have private health insurance instead of a Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer), it says you should check with your insurer in advance which services it covers.

Whether these benefits apply in your own case is decided by your Krankenkasse.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply:
The check-ups are set by the Kinder-Richtlinie (Children's Guideline) of the Gemeinsamer Bundesausschuss. Each Vorsorgeuntersuchung (routine preventive check-up) is called a U-Untersuchung. Children are entitled to these early-detection examinations until they turn 18 (Kinder-RL §1(1)). In the first six years there are ten examinations, and they 'können nur in den jeweils angegebenen Zeiträumen unter Berücksichtigung folgender Toleranzgrenzen in Anspruch genommen werden' (can only be used within the stated periods, allowing for the tolerance limits below) (Kinder-RL §2).

The first check-ups:
- U1: immediately after birth. It should take place within the first 30 minutes after the child is born. 'Birth' here means the birth of the child itself, not the delivery of the placenta. If no doctor is present but a midwife is, the midwife should carry out the U1 (Kinder-RL §3(1)). The table in §2 gives the U1 no tolerance window.
- U2: 3rd–10th day of life (tolerance: 3rd–14th day).
- U3: 4th–5th week of life (tolerance: 3rd–8th week).

The later check-ups, with their tolerance windows (Kinder-RL §2):
- U4: 3rd–4th month (2nd–4½ month)
- U5: 6th–7th month (5th–8th month)
- U6: 10th–12th month (9th–14th month)
- U7: 21st–24th month (20th–27th month)
- U7a: 34th–36th month (33rd–38th month)
- U8: 46th–48th month (43rd–50th month)
- U9: 60th–64th month (58th–66th month)

The same periods apply to babies born prematurely. The guideline says 'Auch bei Frühgeborenen sind die Untersuchungszeiträume einzuhalten'. Prematurity is taken into account when the results are assessed (Kinder-RL §2).

The guideline also contains a temporary exception. It allowed U6, U7, U7a, U8 and U9 to be done outside their periods. That exception ran only 'bis zum Ablauf von drei Monaten ab dem 31. März 2023' (until three months after 31 March 2023) (Kinder-RL §2).

The version quoted here entered into force on 1 January 2026. The G-BA page says the current consolidated version will be published shortly. It also says that a decision in force since 20 August 2026 is not yet reflected in the version offered (G-BA, Kinder-Richtlinie page). Check the G-BA page for the current text.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is a payment for the protection periods before and after the birth, and for the day of the birth itself ("für die Zeit der Schutzfristen vor und nach der Entbindung sowie für den Entbindungstag"). The official family portal says these periods normally begin 6 weeks before the calculated due date and end 8 weeks after the birth.

Who pays depends on your health insurance:

- **Member of a statutory health insurer.** You receive Mutterschaftsgeld under the rules of the Fifth Book of the Social Code (MuSchG §19(1)). If you are employed when the pre-birth protection period begins, it equals your average daily net pay over the last three settled calendar months before that period, capped at 13 euros per calendar day ("höchstens 13 Euro für den Kalendertag"). For other members it is paid at the level of sickness benefit (SGB V §24i(2)).
- **Employer top-up.** If your pay is above 13 euros a day, your employer pays the difference as a top-up ("Zuschuss zum Mutterschaftsgeld"). If you work for several employers, they share it. If your employment is ended under MuSchG §17(2), or your employer cannot pay because of insolvency, the body responsible for paying Mutterschaftsgeld pays the top-up instead (MuSchG §20).
- **Not a member of a statutory health insurer.** You receive Mutterschaftsgeld at federal expense, capped at 210 euros in total ("insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro"). It is paid on application ("auf Antrag") by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung (MuSchG §19(2)).

The claim is suspended while you receive pay subject to contributions, self-employed income or payment in lieu of holiday. This does not apply to one-off payments (SGB V §24i(4)).

Mutterschaftsgeld under the Social Code and the employer top-up, for the time from the day of birth, are offset against Elterngeld. The 210-euro payment under MuSchG §19(2) is not offset (BEEG §3(1)).

**When to apply.** The excerpts do not state an application deadline or a point in time by which you must apply. They say two things about timing:

- For payment before the birth, the deciding document is a certificate from a doctor or midwife that gives the expected date of delivery (SGB V §24i(3)).
- If you are not a member of a statutory health insurer, payment is made on application to the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung.

If you are a member of a statutory health insurer, ask your health insurer how and when to apply. If you are not, ask the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung. These bodies decide on your individual claim.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under German law, being the mother's partner does not by itself make him the legal father if you are not married.

BGB §1592 names exactly three ways a man becomes a child's father ("Vater eines Kindes ist der Mann"):
1. he is married to the mother at the time of the birth ("zum Zeitpunkt der Geburt mit der Mutter des Kindes verheiratet"),
2. he has acknowledged paternity ("die Vaterschaft anerkannt hat"), or
3. a court has determined his paternity ("gerichtlich festgestellt").

The federal family portal puts it plainly: if a father is not married to the mother at the time of the birth, he must make a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) to count as the legal father. It is voluntary and needs the mother's consent.

What the law says about the acknowledgement (BGB §1594):
- It can be made before the child is born.
- It is not effective as long as another man's paternity exists.
- It is invalid if made subject to a condition or a time limit.
- Its legal effects can generally only be claimed from the moment it becomes effective.
- If court proceedings to establish another man's paternity have started, it is not effective while those proceedings are pending, unless it is declared on the court's record under § 180(2) of the Act on Proceedings in Family Matters.

If the mother is married to another man at the time of the birth, no Vaterschaftsanerkennung is possible and her husband is the legal father. The portal notes an exception where a divorce petition was filed before the birth: acknowledgement is then possible within one year after the divorce, with consent of the mother and her (former) husband, and takes effect at the earliest when the divorce is final. The portal marks this information as being updated after a recent change in the law.

Where it is done: the father must make the declaration in person at a competent office, for example the youth welfare office, a registry office, a local court or a notary. The mother must also declare her consent in person. The office records both. Depending on the state, it can cost a fee at a notary or local court.

If the father does not want to acknowledge, or the mother does not consent, the child, the mother or the presumed biological father can ask a court to determine paternity.

Legal fatherhood is not the same as custody. If you are not married at the birth, the mother has parental custody from the birth. Acknowledging paternity does not on its own give the father custody: that also needs declarations by both parents that they want joint custody, or a court decision. Marrying after the birth also establishes joint custody. The family portal says your local youth welfare office advises on custody questions.

One related rule: if only the father is German at the birth and an acknowledgement or court determination is needed to establish descent, the child's German citizenship through him can only be claimed once paternity is effectively acknowledged or determined; the acknowledgement must be made, or court proceedings started, before the child turns 23 (StAG §4(1)).

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
If the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, the mother alone has parental custody at first. BGB §1626a(3) says: "Im Übrigen hat die Mutter die elterliche Sorge."

The father must first be legally recognised as the father. This happens either when he acknowledges the child as his own with the mother's consent, or when a court establishes paternity. Recognition of paternity does not by itself give him custody.

Under BGB §1626a(1), unmarried parents have joint custody in three cases:

1. They declare that they want to take on custody jointly. These are the Sorgeerklärung (declaration of joint custody) declarations: "wenn sie erklären, dass sie die Sorge gemeinsam übernehmen wollen (Sorgeerklärungen)". Both parents must make one. They can be made, for example, at the youth welfare office or before a notary. They can also be made before the birth.
2. They marry each other: "wenn sie einander heiraten". Marrying after the birth also creates joint custody.
3. The family court transfers custody to them jointly: "soweit ihnen das Familiengericht die elterliche Sorge gemeinsam überträgt".

For the court route, BGB §1626a(2) applies. The family court acts "auf Antrag eines Elternteils" (on the application of one parent). It transfers custody, or part of it, to both parents if this "dem Kindeswohl nicht widerspricht" (is not contrary to the child's welfare). If the other parent raises no reasons against joint custody, and none are otherwise apparent, the law presumes that joint custody is not contrary to the child's welfare. According to the Familienportal, the court sets a period for raising such reasons. If none are raised in that period, the court decides in a simplified procedure. In that procedure the youth welfare office is not heard, and the parents are not heard in person.

When Sorgeerklärungen are made, the responsible youth welfare office enters this in a custody register (Sorgeregister). A final court decision transferring custody jointly, in whole or in part, is also entered (SGB VIII §58(1)).

Under SGB VIII §18(2), unmarried mothers and fathers have a right to advice. That advice covers making a Sorgeerklärung and the possibility of a court transfer of joint custody. Your responsible youth welfare office (Jugendamt) gives this advice.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Not simply because the child is born in Germany. Under German law, a child of two foreign parents acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) at birth only if the conditions in StAG §4(3) are met.

The general rule: a child with at least one German parent acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit by birth (StAG §4(1)). For a child of foreign parents, §4(3) applies instead. The child must be born in Germany ("Durch die Geburt im Inland"), and at least one parent must meet both of these conditions:
1. the parent has had their lawful habitual residence in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
2. the parent holds a permanent right of residence ("ein unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or, as a Swiss national or a Swiss national's family member, holds a residence permit under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement of 21 June 1999.

If the child acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit this way, it is entered in the birth register where the birth is recorded (StAG §4(3)).

How it is checked: when the birth is registered, the registry office asks whether a parent holds a permanent right of residence or the Swiss-agreement permit. If the answer suggests the conditions are met, the registry office uses the form in Annex 12 to get written information from the immigration authority. That information confirms whether the details are correct and whether the parent had five years of lawful habitual residence in Germany at the time of the birth. The registry office also requests this information if the parents give no details or if it doubts them. In that case it asks about both parents. The registry office then decides whether the child acquired German Staatsangehörigkeit at birth and records the result (PStV §34(1)–(3)).

Whether your child meets these conditions is decided by the registry office (Standesamt) where the birth is registered, using information from the immigration authority (Ausländerbehörde). It cannot be decided here.

If the child does not acquire German Staatsangehörigkeit, AufenthG §33 sets out the child's residence status:
- A child born in Germany may be granted a residence permit by the authorities on their own initiative if one parent holds a residence permit ("Aufenthaltserlaubnis"), a settlement permit ("Niederlassungserlaubnis") or an EU long-term residence permit ("Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt – EU").
- If at the time of the birth both parents, or the parent with sole custody, hold one of these, the child is granted the residence permit automatically by the authorities.
- If the mother or father holds a visa or may stay without a visa at the time of the birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

The excerpts do not cover whether your child acquires Indian citizenship. For that, contact the Indian embassy or consulate responsible for your area.

rows.question: Does our newborn need a residence permit?
rows.reply:
Federal law sets out three routes for a child born in Germany to foreign parents. Which one applies to your child depends on your own status, and that is decided by the authorities, not here.

1. Residence permit by operation of law (AufenthG §33). The statute contains three rules:
- If one parent holds an Aufenthaltserlaubnis (residence permit), a "Niederlassungserlaubnis" or an "Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt – EU", the child born in Germany "kann … von Amts wegen eine Aufenthaltserlaubnis erteilt werden". It may be granted on the authorities' own initiative.
- If, at the time of birth, both parents, or the parent with sole custody ("der allein personensorgeberechtigte Elternteil"), hold one of those three titles, the child "wird … die Aufenthaltserlaubnis von Amts wegen erteilt". It is granted on the authorities' own initiative.
- If the mother or father holds a visa at the time of birth, or may stay without a visa, the child's stay "gilt bis zum Ablauf des Visums oder des rechtmäßigen visumfreien Aufenthalts als erlaubt". It counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

2. German citizenship by birth in Germany (StAG §4(3)). A child of foreign parents born in Germany acquires German citizenship if one parent meets both of these conditions:
- the parent has lived lawfully and habitually in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
- the parent holds an "unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht", or is a Swiss national, or a family member of one, with a residence permit under the 1999 EU–Switzerland free movement agreement.
The acquisition is entered in the birth register. Separately, under StAG §4(1), a child acquires German citizenship at birth if one parent is a German citizen.

3. Who checks this. When the birth is registered, the Standesamt asks whether a parent holds such a status (PStV §34(1)). Where that is indicated, or where no information is given or there are doubts, it obtains written information from the Ausländerbehörde. This covers whether the details are correct and whether the parent had five years' lawful habitual residence at the time of birth (PStV §34(2)). The Standesamt then examines whether the child acquired German citizenship and records the result (PStV §34(3)).

Whether your newborn is German, receives an Aufenthaltserlaubnis, or is covered by a parent's visa is decided by the responsible authorities. Citizenship is examined by the Standesamt that registers the birth. For the residence permit, the authority is your local Ausländerbehörde.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, as a rule. The law says Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is set off against Elterngeld (parental allowance). BEEG §3(1) lists the income that is "angerechnet" (set off) against Elterngeld. It includes Mutterschaftsgeld under the Fifth Book of the Social Code or the second farmers' health insurance law, and the employer's top-up to Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §20, "die der berechtigten Person für die Zeit ab dem Tag der Geburt des Kindes zustehen" (to the extent they are due for the time from the day of birth).

One exception is stated in the law. The one-off Mutterschaftsgeld of at most 210 euros, paid by the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung to women who are not members of a statutory health insurer (MuSchG §19(2)), is not set off.

The 300-euro amount that BEEG §3(2) otherwise keeps free from set-off does not apply where maternity benefits under §3(1) numbers 1 to 3 are set off.

How the set-off works, according to the law and the federal Familienportal:
- If the maternity benefits are due for only part of a month of the child's life, they are set off only against the matching part of Elterngeld (BEEG §3(1)). The Familienportal explains that maternity benefits are calculated in days, so they are set off to the exact day. For the remaining days of that month, Elterngeld is paid proportionally.
- The Familienportal says maternity benefits for the same child are set off in full. If they are higher than Elterngeld, only the maternity benefits are paid. If Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld on top.
- The Familienportal also says that months in which maternity benefits for the same child are received count as months of basic Elterngeld. One day of entitlement in that month is enough.
- Its example: a child is born on 20 May and maternity benefits end on 14 July. No basic Elterngeld is paid for the first month of life. For the second month (20 June to 19 July), one sixth of the monthly amount is paid (5 of 30 days). From the third month, it is paid in full.
- The Familienportal says the mother's maternity benefits are not set off against the father's Elterngeld, only against the mother's.
- For maternity benefits received for a different child, for example during a new pregnancy while still receiving Elterngeld for the first child, the Familienportal describes a partial set-off. Under that description, 300 euros of basic Elterngeld or 150 euros a month of the Plus variant stay free.
- For mothers with private health insurance who receive sickness daily allowance (Krankentagegeld) during maternity protection, the Familienportal says Elterngeld is set off in full against that allowance. Those months count as months of basic Elterngeld.

This is the general rule. How it applies to your family, and any amount, is decided by the Elterngeld office responsible for your district.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, as long as the work is not full-time. Elterngeld (parental allowance) can be received while working part-time, but income from that work changes the amount.

Who may work. The statute makes it a condition of entitlement that the person "keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit ausübt" (does no work, or does not work full-time) (BEEG §1(1) no. 4). §1(6) says a person is not working full-time if:
1. their working hours do not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the child's month of life ("32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats"),
2. they are in employment for vocational training ("Beschäftigung zur Berufsbildung"), or
3. they work as a suitable childminder within the meaning of §§ 23 and 43 SGB VIII ("geeignete Kindertagespflegeperson").
Under §1(6a), people who are temporarily not working still count as working for this law while they remain in an employment relationship or are self-employed.

How work affects the amount. For months after the birth in which you earn less on average than before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as the applicable percentage of the difference between the two incomes. For this calculation, pre-birth income is counted up to at most 2,770 euros. The difference is calculated separately for months of Basiselterngeld and months of Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §2(3)). The maximum of 1,800 euros a month applies to full months in which the person has no income from work (§2(1)). Elterngeld is paid at a minimum of 300 euros (§2(4)). One month of Basiselterngeld can be exchanged for two months of Elterngeld Plus (§4(3)). The federal family portal says Elterngeld Plus can be especially worthwhile if you work part-time. It also says the Partnerschaftsbonus may be relevant if both parents work part-time at the same time. The portal states that its explanation applies to children born after August 2021, and that partly different rules apply to children born before 1 September 2021.

Reporting income. If the application gives expected income from work during the payment period, the actual income must be proven after that period ends (BEEG §8(1)). If expected income is declared, the amount is decided provisionally until proof is provided (§8(3) no. 3). If the application says you will have no income from work, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case you do have such income (§8(2)). According to the family portal, employees need a certificate from their employer showing their working hours during the Elterngeld period. Self-employed people need their own declaration of their previous working hours and their working hours during the period. Further declarations about how your workload was reduced may be needed. The portal says the employer is obliged to issue the documents you need.

Whether your own work meets these conditions, and how much you would receive, is decided by your Elterngeld office (Elterngeldstelle).

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
How to apply: Kindergeld (child benefit) must be applied for in writing. The law says it is "schriftlich zu beantragen" (BKGG §9(1)). According to the Familienportal, you can submit an electronic or a written application using the Familienkassen form. You can fill in the form online, then print and sign it. For a newborn child, you can apply entirely online with a valid ELSTER certificate, without printing or signing by hand. The application must include your tax identification number (steuerliche Identifikationsnummer) and your child's.

Where to apply: The application should be made at the Familienkasse that is competent under §13 (BKGG §9(1)). Under BKGG §13(1), that is the Familienkasse for the district where the entitled person has their residence (Wohnsitz). The fallbacks, in order, are:
1. With no residence in Germany, the district of their habitual abode (gewöhnlicher Aufenthalt).
2. With neither, the district where they work.
3. In all other cases, the Familienkasse Bayern Nord.

The Familienportal says to apply at the Familienkasse of your Agentur für Arbeit. For questions about applying, it gives the free Bundesagentur für Arbeit service number 0800 4 555530.

Who applies: Kindergeld is paid to only one person per child (BKGG §3(1)). Where a child lives in the joint household of the parents, the parents decide between themselves who the entitled person is. If they make no decision, the family court decides on application (BKGG §3(2)). Besides the entitled person, anyone with a legitimate interest in the payment may also file the application (BKGG §9(1)).

Supporting documents: The Bundesagentur für Arbeit says that for a child under 18 you normally only need to give your tax identification number and your child's. For a child over 18, additional proof is needed, for example a school certificate or internship confirmation. When a child turns 18, the child continues to count only if the entitled person notifies that the conditions of §2(2) are met (BKGG §9(2)). For a child born or living abroad, submit a copy of the foreign birth certificate or another official document certifying the birth. Documents can be sent online to your competent Familienkasse. If more documents are needed, the Familienkasse will tell you the date by which to submit them. Missing that date can delay your application or lead to its rejection.

Retroactive payment: The Familienportal says Kindergeld can be paid retroactively for up to 6 months, if it was due but not paid. To claim this, state in the application that you are applying retroactively and from when you want Kindergeld.

Whether you are entitled is decided by the competent Familienkasse; the decisions on the claim are taken by its management (BKGG §13).

rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply:
Bavaria is outside the states this product covers. We cover federal law, Hessen state procedures and the Indian consular track, so Bavarian procedures are not covered here: where to apply, which forms to use and which office handles your district. For those, contact the Elterngeld (parental allowance) office responsible for your district in Bavaria, or the Bavarian state's official family-benefits portal.

Elterngeld itself is federal law (the BEEG), so the rules below apply in Bavaria as everywhere in Germany.

Who can claim (BEEG §1(1)). You need to meet all four conditions:
1. you live or ordinarily reside in Germany;
2. you live in one household with your child;
3. you care for and bring up the child yourself;
4. you do no work, or not full-time work ("keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit").

Under §1(6), a person is not in full-time work if any of these applies:
1. their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the child's month of life;
2. they are in vocational training;
3. they work as a qualified childminder.

Under §1(6a), self-employed people who are temporarily not working still count as working ("selbständig erwerbstätig").

Income limit (BEEG §1(8)). There is no claim if the parent's taxable income in the last completed assessment period before the birth was more than 175,000 euros. If another person also meets the conditions, for example the other parent, the limit applies to the two incomes combined.

How self-employed income counts (BEEG §2(1)). Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth. It is paid up to a maximum of 1,800 euros a month for full months in which the parent has no income from work. Income from work explicitly includes positive income from "Land- und Forstwirtschaft, Gewerbebetrieb und selbständiger Arbeit" (farming and forestry, a trade or business, and self-employed work). That income must be taxable in Germany. It is reduced by deductions for taxes and social contributions and averaged monthly over the assessment period under §2b. The details are set by §§2c to 2f.

The percentage changes with income (BEEG §2(2)):
- Below 1,000 euros: the percentage rises by 0.1 points for every 2 euros below 1,000, up to 100 percent.
- Above 1,200 euros: it falls by 0.1 points for every 2 euros above 1,200, down to 65 percent.

If you earn less after the birth than before, Elterngeld is that percentage of the difference (§2(3)). Pre-birth income counts at most at 2,770 euros. The minimum is 300 euros, including when there was no income before the birth (§2(4)).

Provisional payment and proof (BEEG §8):
- If you stated expected income in the application, you must prove your actual income for that time after the payment period ends (§8(1)).
- If the tax assessment ("Steuerbescheid") for the last completed assessment period before the birth is not available when you apply, and your application indicates the §1(8) limit will not be exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation if the limit turns out to be exceeded (§8(2)).

Under §8(3), the amount is decided provisionally, based on the information you have made credible, until proof is provided, in any of three cases:
1. the tax assessment is not available and it cannot yet be said whether the §1(8) limit is exceeded;
2. pre-birth income from work cannot be determined;
3. you expect to have income from work during the payment period.

Duration (BEEG §4):
- Parents together are entitled to 12 monthly amounts of basic Elterngeld.
- They get 2 more if one parent's income from work is reduced in two months.
- One month of basic Elterngeld can be taken instead as two months of Elterngeld Plus.
- Each parent must claim for at least two months.

This product cannot say whether you qualify or how much you would receive. Only the Elterngeld office responsible in Bavaria decides your individual case.

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
How much tax you would save by switching tax class is a tax calculation for your household. This product cannot calculate that, and only a Steuerberater or your Finanzamt can advise you on it.

The excerpts do cover a related rule: how a tax class switch before the birth affects the calculation of Elterngeld.

- A change of tax class before the birth "kann sich ... auf die Höhe Ihrer Steuern und Ihrer Sozialabgaben auswirken" (can affect the level of your taxes and social contributions).
- For the simplified calculation of the "Elterngeld-Netto", the newest tax class counts. The older tax class is used only if it applied for longer than the newer one within the whole assessment period. The same applies to other deduction features, such as the number of your child allowances.
- For employment income, the assessment period is "die zwölf Kalendermonate vor dem Kalendermonat der Geburt des Kindes" (the twelve calendar months before the month of birth). Some months are left out of this period. These are months in which the person: 1. received Elterngeld for an older child in certain periods, 2. could not be employed during maternity protection periods or received maternity benefit or certain sickness daily allowance, 3. had an illness mainly caused by the pregnancy, or 4. did military or civilian service. On application, these months can be counted after all (BEEG §2b(1)).
- The income tax deduction is based on the tax class and any factor under § 39f of the Income Tax Act. Tax class VI is not taken into account: "die Steuerklasse VI bleibt unberücksichtigt" (BEEG §2e(3)).
- If you work after the birth, your income after the birth is calculated with the same deduction features as before the birth. Switching tax class again after the birth therefore no longer affects your Elterngeld.

The Elterngeldstelle calculates the Elterngeld-Netto itself, using a simplified procedure. It decides the amount in your individual case. For the tax effect of switching tax class, contact a Steuerberater or your Finanzamt.
